articles.title: Single X-ray pulse reveals plasma nanostructures across scales with one camera
articles.dek: Understanding instabilities and turbulence in plasmas is one of the key challenges across a wide range of plasma research fields, including nuclear fusion, astrophysics and…
paragraphs: Understanding instabilities and turbulence in plasmas is one of the key challenges across a wide range of plasma research fields, including nuclear fusion, astrophysics and laser-plasma physics. In plasmas, slight disturbances can grow due to instabilities, and energy is transferred between structures of various sizes due to turbulence. These phenomena give rise to structures ranging from very small to large, which significantly influence the overall motion and energy flow of the plasma.

Since structures generated by instabilities and turbulence vary with even slight differences in conditions, it is not easy to reproduce the same state in every experiment. Therefore, there is a need for "spatially multiscale single-shot measurements" that can simultaneously capture structures of a wide range of sizes in a single measurement. In particular, in high-energy-density plasmas, instabilities grow in an extremely short time, so high temporal and spatial resolution is also required to capture their initial stages.

By combining the newly developed "beamstop-free X-ray small-angle scattering method" with an X-ray free-electron laser and a microscale rod assembly target, an international research group, led by Assistant Professor Masato Ota of the National Institute for Fusion Science (then a graduate student at the Graduate School of Science, Osaka University), Associate Professor Yoichi Sakawa of the Institute of Laser Engineering, Osaka University, succeeded in measuring the structural collapse and rarefaction processes of high-energy-density plasma across a wide range of spatial scales—from 10 nm to 500 nm—with sub-picosecond temporal resolution.
The findings are published in the journal Communications Physics .
This is the first time in the world that structures across such a wide range of spatial scales have been measured simultaneously using a single X-ray pulse and a single camera.

In conventional small-angle X-ray scattering, the central portion of the beam is shielded by a beam stop to protect the camera from the intense X-ray beam, and the small-angle diffraction patterns appearing around it are measured. However, with this method, it is fundamentally impossible to obtain signals from the ultra-small-angle region hidden by the beamstop.

In the newly developed beamstop-free X-ray small-angle scattering method, a light-attenuation filter system—composed of stacked metal foils optimized for thickness, size and shape—was employed to expand the intensity range measurable by a single X-ray camera to more than 100 times that of conventional methods.

This allows the intense X-ray beam at the center to be attenuated to the camera's measurable range, enabling the simultaneous acquisition of a wide range of diffraction signals—including those from the ultra-small-angle region—from the target, thereby revealing microstructures that could not previously be measured.

The experiments were conducted using a high-brightness, short-pulse X-ray beam generated by the SACLA (SPring-8 Angstrom Compact free electron LAser) X-ray free-electron laser in Harima, Hyogo Prefecture, and a high-intensity femtosecond pulsed laser installed at the same facility.

The researchers used a high-intensity laser to instantaneously transform a silicon microscale rod assembly target—consisting of submicrometer-scale cylinders arranged in a regular pattern—from a solid to a plasma state, and observed the process of structural collapse and rarefaction as changes in the X-ray small-angle scattering signal on picosecond time scales and nanometer spatial scales.

The X-ray beam directed at the rod assembly is diffracted by the individual rods, and the diffracted waves interfere, forming characteristic periodic peak signals on a distant detector. The intensity of the diffraction peaks decreases by several orders of magnitude from low to high order.

Therefore, to selectively attenuate the relatively high-intensity low-order diffraction peaks, the team installed an attenuation filter system in front of the detector, in which the filters were made thicker toward the center to reduce transmittance. This allowed the team to detect a wide range of diffraction peaks, from low to high order, within the detector's dynamic range and measure them simultaneously.

articles.title: How flare ribbons reveal hidden solar explosions on the sun
articles.dek: Many topics in astronomy and astrophysics are esoteric. There's not much of a relationship between something like the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way…
paragraphs: Many topics in astronomy and astrophysics are esoteric. There's not much of a relationship between something like the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way and the life of a regular person going about their business. But the sun is different. Its presence in our lives is inescapable. Its behavior, especially its flaring, has an impact.

Solar flares make themselves known on Earth when their accompanying coronal mass ejections (CME) strike Earth and create mesmerizing auroras. But they can be more than beautiful manifestations of light and magnetic fields. They can pack a punch, especially when they're powerful.

Astrophysicists classify solar flares by their X-ray brightness. From least energetic to most energetic, they're placed in categories A, B, C, M and X. Each letter indicates a tenfold increase in energy output.

A solar flare is a kind of explosion, and solar flares are the most powerful explosions in the solar system. They release an enormous amount of energy, equivalent to the simultaneous detonation of millions or even billions of hydrogen bombs. They dwarf supervolcano eruptions on Earth and even the huge asteroid that ended the dinosaurs.

They're caused by the sun's powerful magnetic fields, which are constantly twisted and rotated. Their specific trigger is reconnection , when the magnetic fields can no longer put up with the twisting and rotating and finally snap. They reconnect into a more straightforward and stable configuration. When that happens, some of the sun's energy is released from its magnetic restraints and emitted as a solar flare.

Solar flares can cause radio blackouts when they strike the ionosphere, disrupting aviation and maritime communications. They can introduce inaccuracies in GPS systems by altering the altitude of satellites. They can sometimes create malfunctions in electronics on spacecraft. Their accompanying CMEs can also disrupt our power grids.

There's an ongoing effort to understand solar flares, and research published in The Astrophysical Journal is part of the effort. It's titled "Evolution of Spatial Complexity in Flare Ribbon Substructure and Its Relationship to Magnetic Reconnection Dynamics." The lead author is Marcel Corchado Albelo from the U. S. National Science Foundation and an ambassador for the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope.

Flares originate in the sun's outermost layer, the corona, which is hidden by the sun's glare, and they're difficult to observe there. But in this research, the authors focused on flare ribbons. These are kind of like a flare's footprints, made of plasma and high-energy particles that slam back into the sun during reconnection. They follow magnetic field lines, and when they collide with the sun's chromosphere, they light up brilliantly.

"Recent three-dimensional flare models suggest that flare ribbon substructure is linked to the fragmentation of the reconnecting current sheet in the corona," the authors write. "Flare ribbon substructure can therefore potentially serve as a unique diagnostic tool for physical processes in the flare current sheet."

The researchers figured out how to quantify the evolution of these flare ribbons and their substructure by looking at small details of the flare ribbons where they deposit their energy in the chromosphere. These details provided clues to what's happening far above.

They created a model and tested it against synthetic observations. Then they applied it to a real flare. "We then apply it to an M6. 5-class solar flare on June 22, 2015, observed by the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS)," the authors write. IRIS is a solar observation satellite launched in 2013.

They found that when the flares deposit their energy, it's not a smooth or uniform process. Instead of one big energetic event, the flare ribbon breaks apart into different-sized fragments and deposits its energy in bursts.

"For the first time we have experimentally shown a physical relationship between the irregular shapes we observe and the structure of the energy conversion region," lead author Corchado Albelo said in a press release .

articles.title: 'One-positron cyclotron' could test a key prediction of the Standard Model
articles.dek: The positron is the antimatter counterpart of the electron, identical in mass but carrying an equal and opposite electric charge.
paragraphs: The positron is the antimatter counterpart of the electron, identical in mass but carrying an equal and opposite electric charge. Like the electron, it also behaves like a tiny bar magnet, and according to a key prediction of the Standard Model of particle physics, its magnetic moment should be exactly equal and opposite to the electron's.

Through new research published in Physical Review Letters , Gerald Gabrielse and colleagues at Northwestern University in Illinois have unveiled a promising new way to test this assumption, by trapping a single positron in a "quantum cyclotron."

The prediction stems from a principle called CPT symmetry . It states that if we swapped every particle for its antiparticle (C), flipped the universe into its mirror image (P), and ran time backward (T), all at once, the laws of physics would be unchanged. In the process, observers like us likely wouldn't even notice.

One of the most sensitive tests of this principle would be to compare the positron's magnetic moment with that of an electron. If any difference emerged between the two values, it would hint at new physics beyond the Standard Model.

However, while electron measurements have reached an accuracy of around 1 part in 10 trillion, the best positron comparison is several orders of magnitude less precise. The main obstacle is getting a positron into an environment isolated and cold enough to make far more precise measurements possible.

In their study, Gabrielse's team tackled this challenge by taking positrons from a radioactive sodium source, which flings them out at extremely high speeds, before slowing them down dramatically. To confine a single positron, they first let it pair up with an electron to form an electrically neutral atom called positronium, which was torn apart inside the trap, leaving the positron behind.

Here, the antiparticle was held in a " Penning trap ," which uses electric and magnetic fields to keep the particle circling on the spot—much like a miniature version of the cyclotrons used in particle accelerators. The trap was then cooled to just a fraction of a degree above absolute zero, allowing the positron to settle into its lowest-energy circling motion.

With the positron's energy now divided into distinct, clearly separated steps, the team could nudge it up and down one step at a time using microwaves and track flips in its spin: the property linked to its magnetism. Crucially, they read out these states by monitoring tiny shifts in the positron's back-and-forth bobbing within the trap, allowing them to detect both its motion and spin without disturbing either.

Once captured, the positron can be stored for several months. This paves the way for future experiments that could measure its magnetic moment with an accuracy rivaling existing electron measurements—potentially around 30 times better than before.

In turn, this first-ever demonstration of a "one-positron quantum cyclotron" could enable the most stringent tests yet of CPT symmetry and a powerful new way to probe the predictions of the Standard Model.

articles.title: Popular Sleep Supplement Could Come With an Unexpected Catch, Scientists Warn
articles.dek: A cannabis compound sold to help people sleep caused withdrawal symptoms in mice after just three days of repeated use.
paragraphs: A cannabis compound sold to help people sleep caused withdrawal symptoms in mice after just three days of repeated use.

Researchers at the University of Connecticut found that repeated doses of cannabinol, or CBN, produced tolerance and withdrawal symptoms in mice. The study, published in Drug and Alcohol Dependence , raises questions about a substance whose popularity as a sleep aid has outpaced research into its risks.

“CBN is everywhere right now. Gummies, tinctures, capsules, and it’s marketed as a safe, herbal sleep supplement,” says Steven Kinsey, a professor in UConn’s Elisabeth DeLuca School of Nursing. “Our findings suggest consumers should be aware repeated use may carry risks.”

Like THC (tetrahydrocannabinol) and CBD (cannabidiol), CBN occurs naturally in cannabis. It is generally described as less psychoactive than THC, but the researchers found that it acts on some of the same biological systems involved in cannabis dependence.

Mice given CBN twice daily for three days developed tolerance, meaning the drug’s effects weakened with repeated exposure. They also displayed withdrawal signs when it was removed, including head twitches and paw fluttering that the researchers compared with trembling hands in people.

A separate experiment examined whether mice could distinguish CBN’s effects from those of THC. Animals trained to respond in a particular way after receiving THC responded similarly to CBN, suggesting the substances produced comparable internal cues. These findings suggest that milder intoxicating effects do not necessarily mean a lower risk of dependence.

“The marketing of minor cannabinoids is pretty wild right now. There are so many therapeutic claims about these drugs, but we really don’t know much about their potential risks, especially with repeated use,” says lead author Olivia Vanegas, who earned her Ph. D. at UConn in 2026.
Although CBN is increasingly sold to help people sleep, little is known about the quality of that sleep or the consequences of regularly taking the doses used in sleep products.

Whether regular CBN use can lead to addiction remains unknown, but the history of sleep aids gives researchers a reason to investigate. Some drugs once promoted for a better night’s rest later proved dangerously habit-forming, making CBN’s unanswered safety questions harder to ignore.

The researchers also observed anti-inflammatory effects at lower CBN doses that did not produce psychoactive effects in the mice. During a simulated bacterial challenge, however, CBN dampened the immune response, suggesting that its effects on inflammation could also influence the body’s defenses against infection.

Researchers still need to determine when CBN’s effects might be useful and when they might create risks. Kinsey emphasizes that the study involved mice, leaving substantial uncertainty about its effects in people, particularly at high doses or with prolonged use.
“CBN may still have therapeutic value,” he says. “But until we know more about dosing and long-term effects, the message for consumers is simple: buyer beware.”

articles.title: Researchers Find That Arthritis May Leave a Hidden Memory in Your Joints
articles.dek: Arthritis may leave a memory in the joints, and mouse experiments suggest stress can reawaken it with help from the body’s heat-producing fat.
paragraphs: Arthritis may leave a memory in the joints, and mouse experiments suggest stress can reawaken it with help from the body’s heat-producing fat.

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) can flare in previously affected joints even after the disease has gone into remission. Psychological stress has long been associated with worsening symptoms, but how it might help inflammation return to those joints has remained unclear.

A study in mice now points to a chain of signals linking the nervous system, heat-producing fat, and cells in the joints. Blocking parts of that chain reduced stress-triggered arthritis in the animals, suggesting a possible direction for future treatments.

The study was led by Assistant Professor Shigeru Tanaka and Professor Hiroshi Nakajima at Chiba University in Japan, in collaboration with two Japanese hospitals. The findings were published in Science Advances on October 16, 2026.

The researchers used a mouse model in which arthritis entered a remission-like state before the animals were exposed to restraint stress. Joint inflammation returned after that exposure. To trace the signals responsible, the team analyzed tissues, profiled immune cells, and measured molecular changes.

Stress activated the sympathetic nervous system, which helps coordinate the body’s stress response, and brown adipose tissue (BAT), a type of fat that produces heat. This activation prompted the brown fat to release interleukin-6 (IL-6), an inflammatory signaling protein. Circulating IL-6 then acted on fibroblast-like synoviocytes, specialized cells in the synovial tissue surrounding the joints.

In response, these joint cells produced CXCL1, a chemokine that attracts immune cells. CXCL1 drew in neutrophils, a type of white blood cell involved in inflammation, contributing to the return of arthritis.

“Our findings suggest that the effects of psychological stress on arthritis extend beyond the immune cells traditionally associated with autoimmune disease. Instead, stress can activate processes within other tissues that contribute to the return of joint inflammation,” Tanaka explains.

The team tested whether interrupting this sequence could reduce the flares by blocking key receptors and monitoring inflammatory markers, joint swelling, and immune-cell accumulation. Treating the mice with a β3-adrenergic receptor antagonist, a substance that blocks that receptor, reduced IL-6 levels in blood plasma, joint swelling, CXCL1 expression, and the accumulation of neutrophils in the joints. Blocking CXCR2, the receptor that responds to CXCL1, also significantly reduced stress-triggered arthritis in the mouse model.

The findings suggest that previously affected joint tissue may retain a form of inflammatory memory that stress can reactivate independently of lymphocytes, a group of immune cells. This offers a possible biological explanation for how inflammation can return to joints after arthritis has subsided.

To examine whether the pathway might also be relevant to people, the researchers compared perceived stress and disease activity in patients with RA. Patients carrying Trp64Arg, a specific variant of the ADRB3 gene that makes cells less responsive to stress-related hormones, showed a weaker relationship between perceived stress and arthritis activity than patients without the variant. The human analysis was observational, however, so it does not establish that stress directly caused changes in disease activity.

Understanding this pathway could eventually help researchers develop strategies to improve disease management and quality of life for people with RA. Its potential as a treatment target remains to be explored.
“Our findings suggest that targeting the stress-responsive pathways may offer a future therapeutic strategy that acts without broadly suppressing the immune system,” Nakajima notes.

articles.title: Newly identified protein pathway helps HIV stay hidden despite treatment
articles.dek: by University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill School of Medicine
paragraphs: by University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill School of Medicine

Current HIV medicines are effective at suppressing the virus in the blood. However, HIV can remain "asleep" or dormant inside certain immune cells and in the brain. These hidden pockets of virus, called HIV reservoirs, are the main reason HIV cannot be cured with today's treatments.

"Our study reveals how human proteins help keep HIV dormant and identifies a pathway that may be targeted in future cure research. Understanding these mechanisms brings us closer to developing strategies to eliminate persistent HIV," said Waqas Ahmed, Ph. D. , a postdoctoral scholar in the lab of Guochun Jiang, Ph. D. , at the UNC HIV Cure Center and the Department of Biochemistry & Biophysics.

In a study published in Cell Reports , Jiang and his research team found that three human proteins—ENL, USP7 and BRD4—work together to maintain HIV latency, keeping the virus quiet and hidden. When researchers disrupted ENL or USP7, they were able to reactivate latent HIV in peripheral blood and brain immune cells called microglia , isolated from people with HIV who are on antiretroviral therapy.

Ahmed's next step is to study the newly identified pathway to see how it works and to evaluate whether targeting ENL or USP7 is safe and effective. Researchers also want a better understanding of how these pathways function in different cell types, particularly in the brain.

"Targeting the ENL–USP7–BRD4 pathway offers a new way to disrupt hidden HIV reservoirs as part of a broader cure strategy. This research could help guide the development of future strategies aimed at eliminating HIV reservoirs that persist despite effective treatment," said Jiang, who is also the corresponding author.

This study shows how human proteins help HIV hide, giving scientists a roadmap to develop strategies that expose and eliminate reservoirs that persist. Researchers also note that because BRD4 plays an important role in several cancers, these findings could inform future cancer research.

"Because BRD4 is a key oncogenic driver in multiple cancers, our discovery has significant translational potential for cancer therapy by targeting USP7 for degradation, thereby eliminating BRD4 protein," said Jiang.

articles.title: Nanoscale alloy redesign tackles cold brittleness for potential deep-space and deep-sea applications
articles.dek: Metallic materials used in extremely cold environments must maintain high strength, ductility and fracture toughness to support applications in aerospace, clean energy,…
paragraphs: Metallic materials used in extremely cold environments must maintain high strength, ductility and fracture toughness to support applications in aerospace, clean energy, superconducting systems and deep-space exploration. However, traditional alloys often suffer performance degradation at ultralow temperatures because of the long-standing trade-off between strength, ductility and toughness. Although metals may become stronger at lower temperatures, they can also become more brittle and prone to fracture.

The sinking of the Titanic is a well-known historical event associated with low-temperature brittle failure. This vulnerability, known as "cold brittleness," remains a bottleneck in the development of deep-sea and deep-space exploration technologies.

A research team led by Zibin Chen, assistant professor in the Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU), has achieved two breakthroughs in addressing this challenge.

Using a nanoscale interface strategy to adjust a metal's internal microstructure, the team developed metallic materials that achieve an unprecedented combination of strength, ductility and toughness at ultralow temperatures of 77 K, equivalent to approximately −196°C.

Building on this work, the team also integrated additive manufacturing, commonly known as 3D printing, with tailored post-processing to develop a nano-architecture strategy. Published in two successive studies in Nature Communications , these advances provide a high-performance, scalable material foundation for next-generation deep-sea and deep-space exploration equipment.

To address the long-standing challenge of cold brittleness in alloys, Chen and his team pioneered a "negative-curvature interface" (NCI) strategy. By changing the surface geometry of nanoscale particles within an alloy, the team enabled the material to withstand high loads while retaining the ability to deform, reducing the likelihood of sudden fracture.

The resulting multi-principal element alloy (MPEA), composed of nickel, cobalt, chromium, aluminum and tantalum (NiCoCr-AlTa), achieves an unprecedented combination of strength, ductility and toughness at liquid-nitrogen temperatures, setting a new benchmark for cryogenic alloys.

Additionally, it can be fabricated using conventional smelting, rolling and short-term aging, without relying on complex new manufacturing methods. This provides a solid foundation for future large-scale production and engineering applications. The team will next validate industrial-scale samples, with the aim of translating the research into commercial applications within the next 10 years.

Chen said, "Our NCI strategy transforms internal precipitates, tiny particles dispersed within the metal, from passive strengtheners into active tunable agents that regulate how the material deforms under load. This concept is applicable across all precipitation-hardened alloy systems, including superalloys, age-hardening steels and aluminum alloys.
"This work opens up a new dimension in advanced material design, offering a cost-effective and scalable pathway for designing high-performance structural materials for industrial applications."

The design was inspired by the energetic evolution during nanoparticle coarsening. Working at the nanoscale, the team proposed constructing NCI on coherent nanoprecipitates, creating specially curved interfaces on the surfaces of particles within the alloy to influence its internal structural response.

As the material deforms under load, numerous partial dislocations, small-scale defects in the crystal structure, form dynamically, producing hierarchical stacking faults (SFs) within the alloy. These layered structural features enhance the material's mechanical performance.

PolyU's advanced aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy and mechanical property evaluation systems enabled the team to observe and characterize these novel microstructures and assess their mechanical performance.

The dense hierarchical SFs significantly enhance the material's strain-hardening capacity and damage tolerance. As a result, the NiCoCr-AlTa MPEA delivers a record-setting combination of cryogenic mechanical properties: a yield strength of approximately 1. 30 GPa, an ultimate tensile strength of approximately 1. 80 GPa, a tensile ductility of 50% and a fracture toughness of approximately 213 MPa·m¹/².

articles.title: Seabird family tree predicts which species accumulate plastic better than diet, global analysis finds
articles.dek: What seabirds eat might seem like a good starting point for identifying species that tend to accumulate plastic in their digestive systems.
paragraphs: What seabirds eat might seem like a good starting point for identifying species that tend to accumulate plastic in their digestive systems. Yet a recent global analysis suggests that mapping the evolutionary relatives of birds could offer better clues than their diets or feeding methods alone.

Researchers at the University of Queensland, London's Natural History Museum and other institutions assembled records covering 93,281 birds belonging to 240 distinct species. In their models, outlined in Biology Letters , evolutionary relationships were found to be the strongest predictor of plastic occurrence in seabirds.

In contrast, the birds' diet, feeding method, body size and specialization in open-ocean feeding showed no consistent effects after the researchers accounted for relatedness and differences among studies.

The researchers combined information from 262 sources published between 1958 and 2024. They focused on the proportion of birds in each sample that presented signs of having consumed plastic, rather than the number of plastic pieces each bird contained.
This widely available measure, known as frequency of occurrence, allowed the team to compare the findings of many studies.

They found that plastic had been recorded in 182 of the 240 sampled species. This means that about three-quarters of sampled species (not individual birds) had at least one record of plastic ingestion.

The researchers then produced models using records covering 82,406 birds from 230 species. They excluded species lacking complete ecological information and samples consisting solely of nest-bound chicks, which do not forage for themselves.

The team compared records of plastic occurrence with the species' lifestyles and positions on an evolutionary family tree, which represents their shared ancestry. Their models accounted for differences in the sampling methods employed across studies, study years, publications, the age groups of the birds and the ocean basins considered.
Closely related species tended to show similar patterns of plastic occurrence. "This does not mean ecological traits are unimportant," the researchers wrote in their paper.

Related species often share feeding habits and other characteristics, including traits that the analysis did not measure. The broad categories used in the analysis to describe a species' lifestyle may also miss finer differences in behavior.

Swallowing plastic and retaining it in the gut are different processes. Some seabirds expel indigestible material in pellets, while others retain it and excrete it slowly. A bird with little plastic in its stomach could therefore have swallowed as much as one that contains more in its gut.

These differences in the processing of indigestible materials are also linked to evolutionary relationships. As the researchers lacked comprehensive information about gut retention rates in different species, retention remains a possible explanation for the observed patterns, rather than a mechanism established across all the species studied.

The team's analysis captures the combined effects of ingestion and retention without measuring them separately. It also cannot establish how much plastic birds encounter, as they may have swallowed debris far from where they are sampled.

Detecting plastic does not reveal its quantity or the harm it causes. Moreover, samples often came from stranded birds or birds caught in fishing gear, potentially overrepresenting unhealthy or stressed individuals.

articles.title: Scientists Find That Cats and Their Owners Share a Surprising Biological Connection
articles.dek: The comfort you find in a cat’s company may have less to do with years together than with everyday closeness, a small observational study suggests.
paragraphs: The comfort you find in a cat’s company may have less to do with years together than with everyday closeness, a small observational study suggests.

Cat owners often credit their pets with making life better, but research has produced mixed evidence about whether owning a cat benefits human health and well-being. Some studies have found positive effects, while others have reported possible negative ones.

Researchers at Kyoto University wondered whether those differences might reflect the quality of the relationship between people and their cats, particularly their everyday interactions. To investigate, the team followed the daily lives of 29 cats and their 19 owners for one month, recruiting participants through flyers and social media. They assessed owners’ moods through questionnaires and observed how the cats behaved toward their owners and unfamiliar people.

To measure everyday physical closeness, the researchers attached small Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) beacons to the cats’ collars. Owners who spent more time physically close to their cats tended to report more positive feelings. How long they had owned their cats, however, was not associated with those positive mood states. The distinction suggests that daily contact may matter more to this aspect of owners’ well-being than the length of the relationship.

Urine samples from both cats and owners revealed connections involving oxytocin, a hormone associated with social relationships, and cortisol, a hormone associated with stress. Higher oxytocin concentrations in cats’ urine were associated with higher oxytocin concentrations in their owners’ urine. Cats with higher oxytocin levels also tended to have owners with lower cortisol levels and fewer negative feelings. The cats’ oxytocin levels were more closely associated with their owners’ negative mood states than the owners’ own oxytocin levels were.

“I think many cat owners are familiar with the sense of comfort and peace they feel when their cat climbs onto their lap seeking affection, they start to pet it, and the cat begins purring contentedly,” says corresponding author Saho Takagi. “Our findings suggest that this feeling may be partly reflected in the hormonal connection between cats and their owners, particularly through oxytocin, a hormone involved in the formation of parent-child bonds and social relationships.”

The findings offer a possible explanation for the inconsistent evidence about cat ownership and health. Benefits or drawbacks may depend on the relationship between a person and their cat, rather than ownership alone. However, the study establishes associations, not cause and effect. The team hopes to explore more deeply how cats and humans influence each other through their everyday interactions.

This work was supported by the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science Research Fellowship for Young Scientists (grant no 22KJ2970) and a Grant-in-Aid for Transformative Research Areas (A) (grant no 26A102), both awarded to S. T. , by the Ayako Ueda Fund Research Grant Program of the Japanese Society of Feline Medicine, and by the Hakubi Project at Kyoto University.

articles.title: New Research Reveals Cows Have a Little-Known Ability To Recognize Humans
articles.dek: A stranger’s face can hold a cow’s attention longer than a familiar handler’s, video tests suggest, offering clues to how cattle recognize the people around them.
paragraphs: A stranger’s face can hold a cow’s attention longer than a familiar handler’s, video tests suggest, offering clues to how cattle recognize the people around them.

When cows watched videos of people, they looked longer when the face on screen matched the voice they heard. The finding suggests that these highly social animals, which live in close contact with humans, can connect a person’s appearance with their voice.

Océane Amichaud of INRAE in Nouzilly, France, and colleagues tested these abilities in 32 Prim’ Holstein cows ( Bos taurus taurus ). Their study, published in the open-access journal PLOS One , examined both how the animals responded to human faces and whether they could link information from sight and hearing.

In the visual tests, the researchers played muted videos of familiar and unfamiliar male faces and measured how long the cows watched them. Unfamiliar faces held the animals’ gaze longer than a familiar handler’s face. That preference for new faces indicated that the cows could distinguish between people they knew and people they did not.

The researchers also tested cross-modal recognition, the ability to connect information received through different senses. They showed videos of familiar and unfamiliar faces while playing a recording of one of the two men speaking. Each man said the same sentence, keeping the words consistent across the recordings.

“In this study, using visual preference and cross-modal tests, we showed that cows are able to process human faces presented in 2D on videos and to associate familiar and unfamiliar faces with the corresponding voices by integrating multiple sensory modalities,” the authors said.

Heart rate measurements taken while the cows watched the videos did not reveal evidence that familiar or unfamiliar faces and voices affected their emotional responses. Differences in how long the animals looked therefore did not correspond to an emotional change detectable through this measure.

The authors caution that watching a video and hearing a recording are not equivalent to interacting with a person. Although the results suggest that cows can identify people through their faces and voices, further studies could examine how the animals interact with specific individuals. Understanding those relationships could help guide efforts to support their welfare.

articles.title: Ancient stalagmites reveal exceptions to Asia–South America monsoon seesaw over the past 450,000 years
articles.dek: In places like South Asia, Africa and parts of the Americas, monsoon rains supply water for drinking, crops and hydropower for billions of people.
paragraphs: In places like South Asia, Africa and parts of the Americas, monsoon rains supply water for drinking, crops and hydropower for billions of people. Understanding the patterns that monsoons tend to follow can help people plan for drought risks affecting agriculture, reservoirs and hydropower across distant regions.

While past research has established patterns between Asian and South American monsoons, in particular, a better record of past monsoons can help researchers understand when these patterns have broken down in the past and which climate changes might explain those exceptions. A new study, published in Nature , lends insight into these dynamics with the help of stalagmites from a cave in Peru.

Researchers know that Asian and South American monsoons generally behave like a seesaw: one region experiences strong monsoons while monsoons in the other weaken, bringing drier conditions. This occurs seasonally, over the course of a year, but also over much longer timescales of thousands of years. Scientists have linked this to changes in Earth's orbit and axial tilt over time, which affect how much sunlight reaches the surface in different areas.

The authors of the new study write, "The global monsoon is controlled by the location of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) and the strength of incoming solar radiation (insolation) in each hemisphere. For this reason, variations in monsoon precipitation are typically antiphased between the two hemispheres and reflect the mean position of the ITCZ as a direct result of orbital (Milankovitch) forcing."

Past research utilized cave records inferred from stalagmite analysis to trace Asian monsoon changes over roughly 690,000 years and show strong links to orbital cycles. Earlier Southern Hemisphere cave records have been more sparse, generally covering only the last two ice-age cycles. While these records pointed to the seesaw effect, a longer record of rainfall activity in South America would help to support the idea and provide further insight.

In an effort to map out monsoon activity over a longer timescale in South America, the team combined oxygen-isotope measurements from 30 stalagmites in three Peruvian caves near the Andes Mountains, using radioactive dating to establish their ages. The resulting data spanned roughly 450,000 years of summer monsoon variability with a few gaps. The researchers checked the rainfall interpretation against modern cave monitoring, nearby lake sediments and other South American cave records. They then compared the reconstruction with Asian monsoon records, other ancient climate evidence and existing ocean-circulation simulations.

Comparison with Asian records confirmed that the two monsoons usually changed in opposite directions, broadly following Earth's roughly 23,000-year orbital wobble. However, the team identified 10 episodes when the records showed simultaneous weakening or strengthening instead. The shared weakening occurred during several transitions out of ice ages and during some warmer intervals, challenging the simple north–south rainfall seesaw.

The two episodes of shared strengthening occurred during the penultimate ice age, which lasted from roughly 194,000 to 135,000 years ago. The researchers say that the synchronous events lasted for several thousand years before the two records reverted to their previous behavior.

The researchers think that these anomalous synchronized periods might indicate that ocean temperatures, greenhouse gases and temperature contrasts between hemispheres can modify the usual orbital influence. It seems that the global monsoon reorganizes itself in response to these changes, especially during intervals of rapid warming.

The study authors write, "Among the 10 synchronous monsoon events of the past 450 ka, interhemispheric weak monsoon intervals (WMIs) during terminations occur regularly, with a periodicity of about 100 kyr. These interhemispheric WMIs occur within intervals of major increases in atmospheric CO₂ and global temperature, which were intervals of reduced meridional temperature gradient.

"As monsoons are driven by temperature gradients (that is, the temperature-driven pressure differences between land and sea), the global reduction in meridional temperature gradients during terminations may be partly responsible for interhemispheric WMIs."

articles.title: These Giant-Headed Ants Are Breaking a Fundamental Rule of Biology
articles.dek: Bigger animals generally have bigger body parts, but new research reveals that certain ants defy this biological rule.
paragraphs: Bigger animals generally have bigger body parts, but new research reveals that certain ants defy this biological rule.

In the insect world, bigger bodies usually come with bigger body parts. But some ants break this rule in an unexpected way. A massive soldier ant, equipped with an oversized head and powerful jaws, can have smaller antennae than a worker that is only a fraction of its size.

Researchers at the University of Ottawa have discovered that this unusual pattern is widespread among Pheidole ants, a diverse group known for their distinct worker and soldier castes. Although antennae grow in proportion to body size within each caste, their sizes overlap between castes despite major differences in overall body size.
The findings suggest that evolution can alter how individual body parts grow, allowing ants to develop specialized features without following the usual rules of biological scaling.

“It was total serendipity. We were sitting at the microscope and Erica (Erica Vong is a graduate researcher and student at uOttawa and lead author of this study) showed me the antennae of two individuals. One was clearly smaller, yet it turned out to be from the soldier!” says Rajendhran Rajakumar, Associate Professor of Biology at the University of Ottawa.

The smaller antennae belonged to a soldier, while the larger ones came from a worker. “Much like when you are getting your favorite latte, both castes have small, medium, and large sizes of overlapping antennae.”

Using laboratory experiments, field data, and museum collections, researchers examined 565 Pheidole species and found the pattern throughout the genus. Comparisons suggest it may have originated near the common ancestor shared with Cephalotes turtle ants.

“Biologists have long assumed that traits such as antennae generally scale predictably with body size,” Professor Rajakumar says. “Our findings show that evolution can decouple a trait from body size in one context while preserving that relationship in another.”
Antennae allow ants to detect chemical signals, navigate their surroundings, and communicate with nestmates. Their size and shape also influence the arrangement of sensory structures.

“The antenna is not simply getting bigger because the ant is bigger,” Professor Rajakumar explains. “In these colonies, development preserves a flexible range of antennal forms that may help individuals compatibly respond together to changing environmental demands.”

Experiments with Pheidole dentata showed that social signals, juvenile hormone, and an organ involved in regulating body proportions influence this flexibility. By manipulating these factors, particularly the soldier inhibitory pheromone, researchers produced unusual “nanoworkers” and “nanosoldiers.” The nanosoldiers had worker-sized bodies but the enlarged heads characteristic of soldiers.

“Social signals and hormones do more than determine whether an ant becomes a worker or a soldier,” clarifies Professor Rajakumar. “They can also reshape how different traits grow and scale together (or decouple), within castes, between castes, and more broadly across species.”

The results demonstrate how colony conditions can influence individual development, supporting the concept of an ant colony as a superorganism. This flexibility may have contributed to the evolution of specialized castes and the remarkable diversity of ants.

“This work reminds us that evolution is not always a process of adding more or less of the same trait,” Professor Rajakumar concludes. “Sometimes new possibilities emerge when the expected connections between traits are broken and development is reorganized.”

articles.title: Cleaner brick kilns cut pollution, but gains did not reach workers, research finds
articles.dek: Relatively simple changes to the way traditional brick kilns operate in Bangladesh can reduce pollution, save fuel and improve the quality of bricks they produce.
paragraphs: Relatively simple changes to the way traditional brick kilns operate in Bangladesh can reduce pollution, save fuel and improve the quality of bricks they produce.

But research has found that those productivity gains did not translate into better conditions for the people doing the work. The findings come from a multiyear research effort involving Nina Brooks, assistant professor at the U-M School for Environment and Sustainability and affiliate faculty member of the Center for South Asian Studies.

The research began with a question: Could an industry essential to Bangladesh's rapid urban growth, but also a major source of air pollution, become cleaner without requiring kiln owners to make expensive investments in new technology?

The answer was encouraging. But it led to a harder question: If cleaner production also makes businesses more productive and profitable, do workers share in those gains? In the short term, the researchers found, they did not.

Bangladesh is the world's fourth-largest brick producer. Approximately 8,000 traditional kilns supply more than 90% of the country's domestic brick consumption. Brickmaking is also associated with substantial carbon emissions and fine particulate matter, or PM2. 5, which contributes to a global public health crisis. Ambient air pollution is responsible for 4. 9 million premature deaths globally, but 32% of those deaths occur in South Asia.

For Brooks, the research is the culmination of about eight years of work that began during her doctoral studies. Along with her collaborators, she first worked to understand the industry itself, mapping kilns using satellite imagery and machine learning, examining regulation and studying health effects on communities living downwind. That work also revealed the limitations of regulating where brick kilns can be established alone.

"Bangladesh is one of the world's most densely populated countries," Brooks said. "It is not feasible to move brick kilns away from all schools, health facilities and urban centers that may be harmed by the pollution."
The researchers began looking instead at whether existing kilns could operate more efficiently.

Working with kiln owners, managers and workers, the team introduced a set of relatively modest operational changes. These included feeding coal into the kiln more continuously and changing how bricks were stacked so air could circulate more efficiently. Other measures reduced heat loss. None required owners to replace their kilns or purchase major new equipment.

After testing the approach in a small pilot, the researchers expanded it across hundreds of kilns in Bangladesh. The results, published in Science , showed that providing training and technical support on the practices reduced energy use and emissions while lowering fuel costs and increasing the production of higher-quality bricks. Across kilns assigned to the intervention, energy use fell about 10. 5%. Carbon dioxide emissions declined by an estimated 171 metric tons per kiln over a firing season, while PM2. 5 emissions fell by about 0. 45 metric tons.

The effects were greater among kilns that adopted the practices because of the intervention: Energy use declined about 23%, while carbon dioxide and PM2. 5 emissions fell by roughly 20%. The economic benefits were important, too. Kiln owners spent less on fuel and produced a greater share of higher-quality bricks.
When researchers returned the following firing season, adoption had not dissipated; in fact, it had increased.

articles.title: Boo! Feeling scared on Halloween can be fun for children but can sometimes push their limits
articles.dek: Halloween is one of the few holidays centered around children.
paragraphs: Halloween is one of the few holidays centered around children. When else can students come to school dressed like astronauts, monsters and witches, or ring strangers’ doorbells to ask for candy?

Horror’s bloody images lurk in the shadows – from ghouls leering over people’s lawns to skeletons hanging from trees – whether invited or not. Thoughtful adults might wonder, what is the right amount of scary for a child?
As a professor of children’s literature, and a writer of children’s books , I turn to the great author and illustrator Maurice Sendak for a hint.

A child’s mother once told Sendak that her pre-schooler was terrified of his classic 1963 book “ Where the Wild Things Are ,” which brings the reader into the world of an imaginative child, Max, after his mother sends him to his room without dinner. Through his imagination, Max journeys to a world of fantastical creatures called Wild Things.
No matter how many times this mother read “Where the Wild Things Are” to her young child, he screamed.
“What are you, a sadist?” Sendak answered. “Read him something else.”
“Why,” he continued, “ would any one book be right for every child ?”

When considering the benefits and drawbacks of scary books to get in the spirit of Halloween, some possible choices come to mind, along with some reminders to both overly cautious and sometimes careless adults.

To start, Felicia Bond’s 1987 “ The Halloween Performance ,” later republished as “ The Halloween Play ,” is a perfect Halloween picture-book classic, appealing to all ages and offering humor and suspense.
Bond is the illustrator of the 1985 children’s best seller, “ If You Give a Mouse a Cookie ,” and subsequent books. An adorable young mouse features in this Halloween story, as well.
The plot revolves around a mysterious “small but important part” that Roger, a nervous, brown mouse, has landed in the school Halloween performance.
Costumed skeletons and witches don’t bother him – but his jitters about performing on stage do.
Roger overcomes stage-fright to shine in the school performance. He may inspire other children to overcome their own feelings of nervousness at Halloween and make fun memories.
Frog and Toad are Arnold Lobel’s beloved, amphibian best friends from his children’s series published in the 1970s.

Though they have very different personalities, both Frog and Toad enjoy the thrill of playing with fear. In “ Shivers ,” a story in the book “Days with Frog and Toad,” Frog tells Toad a tale about “the old dark Frog” who combs the woods in search of tasty children.
Toad keeps asking, “Is this real?” Frog answers like any good storyteller, “Maybe it is and maybe it isn’t.”
Together the duo enjoy scaring themselves into a teeth-chattering but delightful evening.
They show young readers that, in the right doses, fear can be fun: ask any kid scream-laughing on a roller-coaster.
In another story, “ Dragons and Giants ,” Frog and Toad test their own heroism after reading fairy tales about dragons and giants.
Frog and Toad are both fearful and brave, as most of us are.

Wise children’s stories reinforce the truth that it’s natural to be both, sometimes at the same time. “Frog and Toad” features color illustrations in subtle greens and browns, leaving enough space for kids to imagine new facets of themselves – the timid and the bold.
Fear is inevitably woven into the fabric of children’s lives.
Nightmares, for example, spring from unknown sources, though studies show they are intensified by trauma, emotional disturbances and exposure to violence .
Bad dreams – like scary stories – work as fire drills for the developing brain.

articles.title: NASA, Partners Accelerate Lander Development for 2028 Moon Missions
articles.dek: As NASA returns humans to the lunar surface and establishes a long-term presence on our closest celestial neighbor, the agency and commercial human landing system providers…
paragraphs: As NASA returns humans to the lunar surface and establishes a long-term presence on our closest celestial neighbor, the agency and commercial human landing system providers Blue Origin and SpaceX have streamlined the designs and changed both concepts of operations for its future crewed landers.

Since NASA established initial contracts with Blue Origin and SpaceX for crewed missions to the Moon, the agency has redefined Artemis III to demonstrate rendezvous and docking capabilities between test versions of landers from each provider and the agency’s Orion spacecraft in low Earth orbit next year. In parallel, the companies are also developing crew and cargo versions of their landers for near-term Artemis missions.

“We are executing President Trump’s National Space Policy to complete the long-awaited return of American astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028 and establish a Moon Base,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “We have a proven foundation in SLS and Orion, along with two lunar landers in development with Blue Origin and SpaceX. But NASA has no intention of sitting idly by as all the pieces come together. That is not how Apollo succeeded, and it is not how the near-impossible is achieved. NASA is energized, our core capabilities are being rebuilt, our machine shops are running 24/7, and our experts are in the field attacking the critical path.
We are building a Super Bowl-caliber team to safely achieve these objectives and everything that comes next.”

For the initial crewed missions to the Moon, Artemis astronauts will launch in the agency’s Orion spacecraft on top of the SLS (Space Launch System) rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. During each Artemis mission, a commercial human landings system will link up with Orion before taking two crew members to the lunar surface while two remain aboard Orion. To accelerate development toward a 2028 landing, the Artemis landers and Orion will no longer rendezvous in a near-rectilinear halo orbit around the Moon and instead meet up in an orbit that differs for each partner, informed by their systems.

Both companies are required to perform an uncrewed demonstration mission with their crewed landers prior to the near-term Artemis crewed missions to the Moon. NASA will certify lander systems prior to the crewed missions to ensure safety and mission success.

SpaceX continues to plan for an in-space propellant aggregation approach to transfer super cold, or cryogenic, liquid propellant in space. The company will launch multiple versions of Starship to low Earth orbit prior to the launch of the Starship Human Landing System (HLS) from Florida. Similar to a gas station on Earth, the series of propellant “tanker” Starships in low Earth orbit will transfer propellant to the waiting “depot” Starship. The depot Starship will ultimately fuel the Starship lander for its journey to the Moon.

Under the revised operations, Starship HLS will await Orion and its crew in Earth orbit. The lander and Orion will rendezvous and dock in Earth orbit, then the Starship lander will perform a trans-lunar injection burn to send the combined lander and Orion stack to low lunar orbit. NASA is working to modify Orion to enable Starship to push it to the Moon. The lander will bring two crew members to the lunar surface for several days before delivering them back to Orion for the ride back to Earth.

Propellant aggregation in low Earth orbit allows for flexibility in the crew launch timing on SLS, while a trans-lunar injection burn performed by the Starship lander will enable direct access to low lunar orbit. This new concept of operations using low lunar orbit will significantly lower the amount of propellant Starship needs to aggregate in space while reducing the amount of time it can take for astronauts leaving the Moon’s surface in Starship to link back up with Orion. SpaceX will demonstrate the propellant aggregation approach during the uncrewed demonstration mission.

articles.title: NASA’s Artemis III Mission to Test Future Moon Lander Operations
articles.dek: Before astronauts return to the lunar surface, NASA will first conduct one of the most ambitious and complex test missions in the agency’s history.
paragraphs: Before astronauts return to the lunar surface, NASA will first conduct one of the most ambitious and complex test missions in the agency’s history.

Launching in 2027, Artemis III will send NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano aboard the Orion spacecraft into low Earth orbit to perform a series of demonstrations with test versions, or test articles, of human landing systems being developed by industry partners Blue Origin and SpaceX. During the planned 14-day mission, crews and flight controllers will practice the rendezvous, docking, habitation, and operational procedures that will be essential when Artemis astronauts begin landing near the Moon’s South Pole in 2028.
The mission is designed to reduce risk, validate hardware, and gain operational experience before NASA attempts a crewed lunar landing.

“Every piece of this mission in Earth orbit is designed to reduce risk before we put astronauts back on the Moon,” said Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager. “We’re launching three spacecraft on three different rockets and testing how they operate together — something NASA has never attempted. Every lesson we learn here gets us closer to landing on the Moon in 2028.”

Earlier Artemis missions used only NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket and Orion spacecraft. Artemis III will involve three separate spacecraft launched on three different heavy-lift rockets within a relatively short period of time.

The mission begins with Blue Origin launching a test version of its Blue Moon Mark 2 lander into a circular low Earth orbit approximately 273 miles (237 nautical miles) above Earth. The spacecraft can remain on orbit for up to 30 days providing schedule flexibility. Artemis III is designed as a tightly choreographed campaign, with NASA planning to launch Orion on top of SLS from the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida only days after the Blue Moon test article launch and confirmation the vehicle is healthy and ready for joint operations.

Following launch, Orion will initially enter an elliptical Earth orbit of 18 x 1122 miles (16 x 975 nautical miles). It will use its service module to perform a series of maneuvers to transition to a circular orbit at about 345 miles (300 nautical miles) for thermal stabilization before then gradually setting up its rendezvous with the waiting Blue Moon lander test article. Because each spacecraft operates in slightly different orbital regimes optimized for its mission requirements, Artemis III requires a carefully choreographed sequence of orbital maneuvers and rendezvous operations throughout the flight.

During the first two days of flight, the crew will check out Orion’s systems, prepare for proximity operations, and gradually position themselves for the mission’s first major objective: rendezvous and docking with the Blue Moon test vehicle.

The operation represents NASA’s first opportunity to evaluate how Orion and a commercial lunar lander work together in space. Engineers will assess how software aboard both spacecraft, guidance systems, communications systems, and operational procedures perform in real-world conditions, while flight controllers gain experience coordinating activities across multiple teams and organizations.

Once docked, astronauts will spend approximately two days conducting evaluations aboard the Blue Moon test article. Crew members will open the hatch and enter the spacecraft, allowing them to assess the cabin environment, controls, and life-support systems firsthand. Teams will verify the spacecraft’s ability to maintain the proper atmosphere and pressure.

The Blue Moon test article incorporates many of the avionics, software, flight-control systems, crew-cabin technologies, and life-support functions planned for future lunar missions. Testing those systems in orbit will provide the first opportunity to evaluate how many of the lander’s flight systems perform in space as an integrated vehicle.

By the time Orion undocks, NASA will have completed its first evaluation of a commercial lunar lander with crew, gathering data on spacecraft systems, crew operations, and spacecraft interoperability not possible on the ground.
After completing operations with Blue Origin’s lander, Orion will undock and reposition to support the next phase of the mission: a second rendezvous operation.

articles.title: NASA’s Swift Mission Ends, Leaves Behind Scientific Bonanza
articles.dek: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has ended its science mission now that the spacecraft is orbiting less than 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth’s surface.
paragraphs: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has ended its science mission now that the spacecraft is orbiting less than 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth’s surface. The greater atmospheric drag at this height prevents the satellite’s telescopes from steadily gazing at their astronomical targets.
Swift conducted its final observation on Oct. 20. It is expected to re-enter the atmosphere in the next few weeks.

“Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long,” said Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director, Astrophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “In that time, Swift played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics that showed how critical rapid-response observations are to the entire community.

To support rapid response to cosmic events in a post-Swift world, we’re exploring our ability to use and augment NASA’s fleet of existing space telescopes, from fast-to-orbit commercial capabilities to efficient, innovative new missions. And Swift leaves us with an extraordinary archive of multiwavelength observations that will fuel new discoveries for decades more.”

In its storied career, Swift has observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts , the most powerful explosions in the cosmos. It has studied more than 1,400 supernova explosions, witnessed stars shredded by black holes , monitored active galaxies , conducted an all-sky X-ray survey, studied asteroids and comets , and more. Swift data has contributed to about 7,000 published scientific papers.

“Swift was designed as a satellite dedicated to studying gamma-ray bursts, outbursts that came and went so quickly that no one could target them with large telescopes to learn more,” said S. Bradley Cenko, the mission’s principal investigator at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. “Swift needed to detect and locate gamma-ray bursts, communicate their position to other observatories, and then swing its telescopes around to image the burst locations before their afterglows faded out. This typically took Swift about a minute to do.”

Led by its first principal investigator, Neil Gehrels, Swift was born as a multiwavelength observatory, with co-aligned Optical/Ultraviolet and X-ray telescopes that could quickly image and refine a burst’s position. The mission launched into orbit on Nov. 20, 2004, and went to work the following month. In 2018, NASA renamed the mission to honor Gehrels following his death.

Speed was especially important for an elusive population called short gamma-ray bursts, which reach peak brightness in less than two seconds. Until Swift, it had been impossible to locate these bursts rapidly and precisely enough to observe their afterglows. In May 2005, Swift achieved this milestone with GRB 050509B , which lasted just 0. 03 seconds. Swift turned to the burst fast enough to detect 11 X-ray photons, making this the first short burst with a detected afterglow. These observations validated long-standing theoretical models, showing that short gamma-ray bursts likely come from mergers of two neutron stars — objects with the mass of the Sun that have been crushed to the size of a city.

Another factor led to Swift’s success as a kind of astronomical multitool. Its flexible planning system enabled astronomers to request “target-of-opportunity” observations that could be commanded from the ground in as little as a few minutes, or to set up monitoring programs for observing specific sources lasting from as little as a few minutes to months. The system could schedule up to 75 independent targets a day.

“The unique speed of response of the Swift hardware, the extraordinary success of the rapid mission operations, and the closely knit teamwork of the Swift Flight and Science Operations teams placed Swift at the crossroads of burgeoning areas of research,” said John Nousek, the mission’s operations director and professor of astronomy and astrophysics in the Eberly College of Science at Penn State in University Park, Pennsylvania.

The Swift archive contains nearly 22 years of brightness measurements of all kinds of cosmic outbursts, multiwavelength spectra, more than 1. 5 million images from its Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope, and much more. The full dataset, publicly available as part of NASA’s commitment to open, gold standard science, spans approximately 12 terabytes, the storage equivalent of about 600 high-definition movies.

articles.title: Your Saliva Could Hold the Key to Detecting a Deadly Cancer
articles.dek: Scientists have discovered distinct bacterial patterns in the saliva of patients with a deadly form of esophageal cancer.
paragraphs: Scientists have discovered distinct bacterial patterns in the saliva of patients with a deadly form of esophageal cancer.

Bacteria living in the mouth may hold clues to a deadly form of esophageal cancer that often goes undetected until treatment options are limited. Researchers in South Africa have identified distinctive bacterial patterns in patients’ saliva, raising the possibility that a simple, inexpensive test could eventually help identify people who need further screening.

The study, published in Communications Medicine , was conducted by scientists at the Sydney Brenner Institute for Molecular Bioscience (SBIMB) at Wits University and Columbia University in New York. Combining bacterial DNA sequencing with machine learning, the team developed a model that distinguished cancer patients from unaffected individuals more effectively than one based on clinical and demographic information alone.

Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is especially common in parts of eastern and southern Africa, including South Africa’s Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal provinces. High rates also occur in regions of China and Iran, forming a geographic belt that scientists have struggled to explain.

Unlike esophageal adenocarcinoma, which is strongly associated with acid reflux, obesity, and lifestyle factors, ESCC has less clearly understood causes. It also frequently affects relatively young adults.
“A feature of the cancer is the young age of many patients, with a mean age of 50, and 18% of patients presenting before the age of 40,” says Distinguished Professor Christopher Mathew of the SBIMB.

“This geographical occurrence is also puzzling, and may reflect genetic susceptibility, a specific environmental exposure, or a combination of factors that researchers have still not been able to pin down,” explains Dr. Wenlong Carl Chen, a researcher at SBIMB.

Analysis of data from the Johannesburg Cancer Study identified several ESCC risk factors, including smoking, heavy alcohol consumption, rural residence, lower educational attainment, and the use of biomass or other household fuels.
“Still, they do not fully explain the number of cases, the geographic clustering, or why some patients develop the disease without these obvious exposures.”

To investigate another possible indicator, researchers examined the oral microbiome, the community of microorganisms living in the mouth. DNA sequencing revealed distinct differences between saliva samples from cancer patients and unaffected controls.

“We found clear differences between the saliva bacteria of people with oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma and unaffected controls. Using genetic sequencing of bacteria and machine-learning methods, the team identified a distinctive microbial pattern associated with the cancer,” says Chen.

Several bacterial species were more abundant in ESCC patients, including Fusobacterium nucleatum, a microorganism previously implicated in other cancers. The microbiome-based model also performed better than one relying solely on clinical and demographic data.

However, the findings do not establish that these bacteria cause cancer. The microbial changes could instead result from the disease itself, particularly as a growing tumor narrows the esophagus and disrupts normal swallowing.

“But even that could be useful. A blockage in the esophagus develops gradually, often before patients arrive at the hospital, unable to swallow properly. If microbial changes in saliva can help flag that something is already changing, they could one day help identify people who need earlier referral for endoscopy.”

articles.title: Scientists Discover a Hidden Cholesterol Switch That Could Change How We Treat Heart Disease
articles.dek: Researchers uncovered how a high-cholesterol diet weakens the liver’s defenses and lowered LDL in mice by blocking the pathway, pointing to a potential new use for a shelved…
paragraphs: Researchers uncovered how a high-cholesterol diet weakens the liver’s defenses and lowered LDL in mice by blocking the pathway, pointing to a potential new use for a shelved heart failure drug.

A diet high in cholesterol can gradually weaken the liver’s ability to remove harmful cholesterol from the blood. Cholesterol-related heart disease remains the leading cause of death worldwide, even as doctors have gained more medications to treat it.

Researchers at the University of California San Diego School of Medicine have identified a previously unknown biological pathway that helps explain why the liver’s cholesterol-clearing capacity declines. Their study, published in Nature , combined experiments in mice and human cells and identified a potential treatment target. An experimental drug that acts on that target has already undergone initial safety testing in humans, potentially shortening the route to a clinical trial for high cholesterol.

The liver normally removes cholesterol from the blood so it can be broken down and used elsewhere. Proteins called LDL receptors sit on the surface of liver cells, where they capture harmful low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol and pull it inside for processing. More receptors mean more cholesterol can be cleared. Most cholesterol-lowering drugs, including statins and PCSK9 inhibitors, work by increasing or preserving the number of these receptors.
Some patients, however, cannot tolerate the side effects of available medications.

“There’s still a real need for new cholesterol-lowering options, since some people can’t get to safe levels even with the drugs we have now,” said senior author Alan Saltiel, PhD, professor of medicine at UC San Diego School of Medicine and director of the UC San Diego/UCLA Diabetes Research Center. “This new pathway we discovered is completely separate from anything that existing drugs target, so it gives us a new opportunity to fill that gap.”

The newly identified pathway works against cholesterol removal by gradually depleting LDL receptors. It begins when high dietary cholesterol activates Ral, a protein Saltiel previously studied in fat cells. As Ral activity increases, fewer LDL receptors remain available to pull cholesterol from the bloodstream, contributing to higher blood cholesterol.

That receptor loss ultimately depends on an enzyme called cathepsin A, or CTSA. When the researchers blocked CTSA with a small molecule inhibitor, they stabilized LDL receptors and sharply lowered circulating LDL cholesterol in mice.

“We’ve known for a long time that a high-cholesterol diet reduces the liver’s ability to clear cholesterol from the blood, but we didn’t fully understand why,” said Saltiel. “This new discovery explains a critical piece of that puzzle.”

Turning a biological discovery into a treatment usually requires substantial additional research to find a suitable drug. In this case, a CTSA inhibitor had already been developed as a potential treatment for heart failure. It reached a Phase 1 clinical trial, where it was successfully tested for safety, before being shelved for strategic reasons.
That earlier work could allow the investigational drug to move into a Phase 2 trial for high cholesterol. The reduction in LDL cholesterol demonstrated in mice has yet to be established in people.

“Luckily, there’s an experimental drug sitting on the shelf that’s already been shown to be safe in humans,” said Saltiel. “We hope to test whether this might be effective by conducting a clinical trial — which could potentially bring a new treatment option to patients much sooner than would have been expected.”
